summary: This paper is a narrative review of research on why multilingual language models exhibit zero-shot cross-lingual transfer. It organizes prior work into five factor categories: linguistic similarity, lexical overlap, model architecture, pre-training settings, and pre-training data. Across these categories, the authors synthesize findings from a broad set of studies, highlight recurring agreements and contradictions, and propose explanations for discrepancies, such as differences between synthetic vs. natural language experiments, task type, and modeling choices used in transfer-performance prediction. The paper’s main contribution is a structured consolidation of the literature and a set of practical takeaways, e.g., syntax and other linguistic similarities matter, lexical overlap is often interaction-dependent rather than sufficient on its own, architecture and parameter sharing affect alignment, and pre-training corpus size/source and tokenizer choices influence transfer quality.

This paper is a narrative review of research on what drives zero-shot cross-lingual transfer in multilingual language models. It organizes prior work into five factor categories: linguistic similarity, lexical overlap, model architecture, pre-training settings, and pre-training data. Across these categories, the authors synthesize findings from a broad set of studies, highlight recurring agreements and contradictions, and propose explanations for discrepancies, such as differences between synthetic vs. natural language setups, task type, model family, and feature-importance methodology. The paper’s main contribution is a structured consolidation of the literature rather than new experiments, with practical takeaways about when factors like syntax, lexical overlap, tokenizer quality, model capacity, and target-language pretraining data matter most.

This paper introduces a new task setting for open-world product attribute mining under light supervision: given a small curated seed attribute set and product text (titles plus bullet points), the goal is to both expand values for known attribute types and discover values for previously unseen attribute types. To support this setting, the authors build the WOAM dataset across four Amazon product categories, with 66 total attribute types and 42% unseen types in the test set. They propose Amacer, a pipeline with syntax-based candidate span generation, supervised contrastive learning from seed attributes, adaptive expansion for known attributes, DBSCAN for additional clustering, and two regularizers for unseen-attribute discovery: a self-supervised bullet-point co-occurrence objective and an unsupervised latent-attribute/topic-style reconstruction objective. Experiments show consistent gains over closed-world tagging baselines and OA-Mine variants, with the best reported overall performance reaching 47.6 exact-match F1 and 59.1 partial-match F1 on their pseudo-clustering metric, plus especially strong improvements on new attribute types.

This paper introduces a new task setting for open-world product attribute mining under light supervision. Instead of assuming a fixed attribute schema or requiring explicit descriptions of unseen attributes at inference time, the task aims to both expand values for known seed attribute types and discover values for entirely new attribute types from product titles and bullet-point descriptions. To support this setting, the authors construct a new dataset, WOAM, spanning four Amazon product categories with curated seed attributes and human-annotated test data. The proposed method, Amacer, uses syntax-based candidate span generation, supervised contrastive learning over seed attributes, adaptive expansion for known attributes, DBSCAN for additional clustering, and two auxiliary regularizers for new-attribute discovery: a self-supervised bullet-point co-occurrence objective and an unsupervised latent-attribute reconstruction objective inspired by neural topic models. Experiments show consistent gains over closed-world tagging baselines and OA-Mine-style open-world baselines, with the strongest reported result being 47.6 exact-match F1 and 59.1 partial-match F1 on their clustering-based evaluation, plus improved performance on unseen attribute types.

This paper proposes Grouped Head Attention (GHA) to reduce redundancy in multi-head attention by explicitly grouping heads during training. The method uses a self-supervised Group-Constrained Training (GCT) objective that encourages heads within a group to become similar while pushing different groups apart, using hidden units discovered by clustering head feature maps. After training, a Voting-to-Stay (V2S) pruning procedure keeps one representative 'Pillar of Strength' head per group and removes the others, yielding a compressed model (GHT-PS). Experiments on machine translation, abstractive summarization, and language modeling show consistent gains over vanilla transformers and several prior efficient-attention baselines, with substantial parameter reductions and improved inference efficiency.

This paper proposes Grouped Head Attention (GHA), a modification/training strategy for multi-head attention aimed at reducing redundancy and over-parameterization. The method uses Group-Constrained Training (GCT), a self-supervised objective that clusters heads into groups and encourages intra-group similarity and inter-group diversity based on head feature maps, and a Voting-to-Stay (V2S) pruning procedure that retains one representative 'Pillar of Strength' head per group. Experiments on machine translation, abstractive summarization, and language modeling show consistent gains over vanilla Transformers and several prior efficiency-oriented baselines, while also reducing parameters, FLOPs, and sometimes improving inference speed. The paper also includes ablations and analyses of group compactness and number of groups.

The paper presents a systematic empirical study of task-specific knowledge distillation (KD) for natural language generation under a realistic medium-resource setting with limited labeled data and abundant unlabeled data. Across four English NLG tasks (summarization, question generation, abductive reasoning, and Shakespeare-to-modern-English transfer), the authors compare architectural choices, pruning strategies, KD objectives, and pseudo-target (PT) training variants. The main contributions are: (1) an exposure-bias perspective on NLG distillation; (2) a family of PT augmentation methods that extend standard sequence-level KD beyond a single beam-search target; and (3) a new Joint-Teaching method that applies word-level KD on PTs generated by both teacher and student. Empirically, the study finds that encoder-decoder models outperform decoder-only models for task-specific conditional NLG, decoder pruning is preferable to encoder pruning for latency/performance tradeoffs, unlabeled-data PTs are highly beneficial, multiple sampled PTs outperform single beam PTs, and Joint-Teaching further improves distilled students. The paper also includes an exploratory extreme setup distilling GPT-4 into T5-small without labeled training data, though results there are mixed.

This paper presents a systematic empirical study of task-specific knowledge distillation (KD) for natural language generation under a realistic medium-resource setting with limited labeled data and abundant unlabeled data. Across four English NLG tasks (summarization, question generation, abductive reasoning, and Shakespeare-to-modern-English style transfer), the authors compare architectural choices, pruning strategies, KD objectives, and pseudo-target (PT) training variants. The main contributions are: (1) an exposure-bias-based motivation for PT augmentation in KD; (2) a family of PT extensions beyond standard sequence-level KD, including unlabeled-data PTs, multiple PTs, and sampling-based PT generation; and (3) a new Joint-Teaching method that applies word-level KD on PTs generated by both teacher and student. Empirically, the study finds that encoder-decoder models outperform decoder-only models for task-specific conditional NLG, decoder pruning is preferable to encoder pruning, and PT-based training—especially with unlabeled data, multiple sampled PTs, and Joint-Teaching—substantially improves distilled student performance while preserving large inference-time efficiency gains. The paper also explores an extreme no-labeled-data setup using GPT-4 as teacher, with mixed but partially supportive results.

This paper studies false negatives in vision-language contrastive pretraining and argues, from a mutual-information perspective, that standard InfoNCE effectively maximizes MI between positives while also minimizing MI between anchors and negatives, which is problematic when some negatives are semantically matched or partially matched. The authors derive a generalized lower bound in the presence of false negatives and propose Similarity-Regulated Contrastive Learning (SRCL), which assigns each negative a weight inversely proportional to estimated cross-modal similarity, with similarity progressively refined using a frozen auxiliary model and the current VLP model. Implemented on top of ALBEF, SRCL improves performance on image-text retrieval, zero-shot retrieval, VQA, and NLVR, with qualitative analyses suggesting a more structured cross-modal embedding space.

This paper studies false negatives in vision-language contrastive pretraining and argues that standard InfoNCE is suboptimal when semantically matched or partially matched negatives are present. The authors revisit the mutual-information interpretation of InfoNCE and derive a generalized lower bound suggesting that the objective effectively maximizes MI between anchors and positives while minimizing expected MI between anchors and negatives, which can be harmful when some negatives are actually semantically related. Motivated by this, they propose Similarity-Regulated Contrastive Learning (SRCL), which assigns each negative a weight inversely proportional to estimated cross-modal similarity, with similarity progressively refined during training using a frozen auxiliary model and the current VLP model. Implemented on top of ALBEF, SRCL improves performance on image-text retrieval, zero-shot retrieval, VQA, and NLVR, with consistent gains over the ALBEF baseline.

This paper presents an empirical study of parameter-efficient preference alignment for LLMs, focusing on three axes: alignment dataset, alignment method, and base model type. Using over 300 experiments with LoRA/QLoRA on LLaMA-1, Vicuna-v1.3, Mistral-7b, and Mistral-7b-Instruct, the authors compare SFT and DPO on harmlessness/helpfulness splits derived from HH-RLHF and BeaverTails, and evaluate on MMLU, BBH, AlpacaEval, RealToxicity, and Red-Instruct. The main findings are that higher-quality preference data generally helps, SFT tends to work better for pre-trained models while DPO is stronger for instruction-tuned models and more faithful to explicit preferences like harmlessness, mixing distinct preferences often hurts, and some model-merging strategies can mitigate trade-offs.

This paper presents an empirical study of parameter-efficient preference alignment for LLMs, focusing on three axes: alignment dataset, alignment method, and base model type. Using over 300 experiments with LoRA/QLoRA on LLaMA-1, Vicuna-v1.3, Mistral-7b, and Mistral-7b-Instruct, the authors compare SFT and DPO on harmlessness/helpfulness splits derived from HH-RLHF and BeaverTails, and evaluate on MMLU, BBH, AlpacaEval, RealToxicity, and Red-Instruct. The main findings are that higher-quality preference data generally helps; SFT tends to work better for pre-trained models while DPO is more effective and more preference-faithful for instruction-tuned models, especially on explicit preferences like harmlessness; mixing distinct preferences often hurts; and some model-merging strategies can mitigate trade-offs. Overall, the paper is a broad experimental benchmarking/guidelines paper rather than a methodological contribution.

This paper proposes Masked thought Fine-Tuning (MFT), a simple supervised fine-tuning variant for mathematical reasoning in which random tokens in the chain-of-thought are masked or replaced during training while the original full reasoning remains the target. The authors argue that this acts as a regularizer that discourages over-reliance on nearby tokens and encourages stronger dependence on the original question and earlier reasoning steps. Empirically, across Llama-2 and Mistral base models and several math training datasets (GSM8K, MATH, GSM8K-RFT, MathInstruct, MetaMathQA), MFT generally improves over standard SFT, often by 1.5–5.5 points on GSM8K and modestly on MATH. The paper also shows complementarity with augmented datasets, stronger robustness on GSM-IC distractor settings, and presents analyses suggesting increased long-distance dependency and reduced semantic/incoherent reasoning errors. The method is lightweight and easy to implement, though some claims about mechanism remain largely correlational rather than causal.

This paper proposes Masked thought Fine-Tuning (MFT), a simple modification to supervised fine-tuning for mathematical reasoning: randomly mask some tokens in the chain-of-thought during training while keeping the original target reasoning as supervision. The authors argue that this acts as a regularizer that discourages over-reliance on nearby reasoning tokens and encourages stronger dependence on the original question and earlier steps. Empirically, across Llama-2 and Mistral base models and several math training datasets (GSM8K, MATH, GSM8K-RFT, MetaMathQA, MathInstruct), MFT generally improves over standard SFT, often by 1.5-5.5 points on GSM8K and modestly on MATH. The paper also compares MFT to other noise/regularization methods, studies mask ratio scheduling, reports stronger robustness on GSM-IC distractor settings, and provides analyses suggesting increased long-distance dependency and reduced semantic/incoherent reasoning errors. The method is simple, cheap, and appears complementary to existing data augmentation pipelines, though the mechanistic claims remain largely empirical and some evaluations have confounds.

The paper presents LOGICLLAMA, a LLaMA-7B model fine-tuned with LoRA for natural-language-to-first-order-logic (NL-FOL) translation. It also introduces MALLS, a 34K GPT-4-generated silver dataset of NL-FOL pairs, and a two-stage training framework: supervised fine-tuning on synthetically perturbed FOL examples with chain-of-thought-style correction steps, followed by RLHF using GPT-3.5 outputs and a logical-equivalence-based reward. On LogicNLI and FOLIO, the model outperforms GPT-3.5 in direct translation and, in correction mode, approaches GPT-4-level performance on FOLIO at lower cost.

The paper studies natural-language-to-first-order-logic (NL-FOL) translation using large language models. It introduces LOGICLLAMA, a LLaMA-7B model fine-tuned with LoRA for both direct NL→FOL translation and post-hoc correction of GPT-3.5 outputs. The work also presents MALLS, a 34K GPT-4-generated silver dataset of NL-FOL pairs, created with a prompt pipeline that encourages diversity and syntactic validity. Methodologically, the paper compares direct translation, one-shot correction, and a chain-of-thought (CoT) correction framework trained via supervised fine-tuning on synthetically perturbed FOL rules followed by RLHF using a logical-equivalence-based reward. On LogicNLI and FOLIO, LOGICLLAMA direct translation outperforms GPT-3.5, and the RLHF CoT correction mode approaches GPT-4-level performance on FOLIO while using a much smaller local model.

This paper proposes a pretraining-and-transfer framework for EEG-to-text decoding. The core contribution is CET-MAE, a multimodal self-supervised model that combines masked reconstruction of EEG and text with EEG-text contrastive alignment using a multi-stream encoder. The downstream framework, E2T-PTR, transfers the pretrained EEG-side modules into a BART-based decoder for open-vocabulary text generation from EEG. Experiments on ZuCo reading-task combinations (3, 4, and 5 tasks) show improvements over prior EEG-to-text baselines on BLEU and ROUGE metrics, with ablations suggesting benefits from sentence-level EEG features, the combined SSL objectives, and the multi-stream design.

The paper proposes CET-MAE, a pretraining framework for EEG-text representation learning that combines masked reconstruction of EEG/text with EEG-text contrastive alignment via a multi-stream encoder, and E2T-PTR, a downstream EEG-to-text decoding framework that transfers the pretrained EEG-side representations into a BART-based generator. Experiments on ZuCo reading-task combinations (3, 4, and 5 tasks) show modest but consistent gains over prior EEG-to-text baselines on BLEU and ROUGE metrics, with ablations suggesting benefits from sentence-level EEG features, the combined SSL objective, and the multi-stream design.

This paper studies whether large language models for automated theorem proving can benefit from learning from failed proof attempts, not just successful proof paths. The authors introduce PropL, a Lean-formalized dataset of intuitionistic propositional logic theorems with proof trees generated by a focused proof search procedure, including trial-and-error and backtracking information. They train TRIALMASTER on these proof traces and compare it against a conventional LLM-based prover trained only on correct proofs and paired with DFS at inference. On in-distribution data both methods perform near perfectly, while on an out-of-distribution split TRIALMASTER achieves higher success (88.7%) with lower search cost than strong DFS baselines. Ablations suggest that including failed paths materially improves performance.

This paper studies whether large language models for automated theorem proving can benefit from learning from failed proof attempts, rather than only from successful proof paths. The authors introduce PropL, a Lean-formalized dataset of intuitionistic propositional logic theorems with trial-and-error proof traces generated via a focused proof search procedure. They train TRIALMASTER on proofs that include backtracking and failed search paths, and compare it against a conventional LLM-based prover trained only on correct proofs and used with DFS at inference. On an out-of-distribution split defined by longer proof lengths, TRIALMASTER achieves higher success rate (88.7%) with lower search cost than strong DFS baselines, while on in-distribution data both methods are near-perfect. The paper’s main claim is that incorporating trial-and-error information improves both tactic quality and backtracking behavior.

This paper studies user-side privacy protection for online self-disclosures. It introduces a 19-category taxonomy of self-disclosure, a Reddit corpus of 2.4K posts with 4.8K annotated disclosure spans, and models for span-level disclosure detection, disclosure abstraction, and importance rating. The detection model achieves about 65.7 partial span F1 on the multi-class task, and a user study with 21 Reddit users suggests practical interest in such a tool. Motivated by user feedback, the paper proposes span-level self-disclosure abstraction: rewriting disclosure spans into less specific alternatives while preserving utility. Human evaluation indicates the best abstraction models provide moderate privacy gains with high utility and diversity. The paper also introduces importance rating of disclosures for contextual understanding, with a fine-tuned model reaching about 80% accuracy, comparable to GPT-3.5.

This paper studies user-side privacy protection for online self-disclosures using language models. It makes three main contributions: (1) a fine-grained span-level self-disclosure detection dataset from Reddit with 2.4K posts, 4.8K annotated spans, and a 19-category taxonomy; (2) detection models for identifying disclosure spans, with the best fine-tuned DeBERTa model achieving about 65.7 partial span F1 on the multi-class task; and (3) two new downstream tasks motivated by a user study: self-disclosure abstraction (rewriting disclosures into less specific but still useful language) and importance rating (estimating whether a disclosure should be removed, abstracted, or kept). The paper also includes an HCI interview study with 21 Reddit users, where most participants viewed the tool positively, and human evaluations suggesting the abstraction model can moderately improve privacy while preserving utility. Overall, the work is novel in framing privacy protection around span-level self-disclosure detection and selective abstraction rather than only PII masking or sentence-level classification.

This paper introduces X-Topic, a multilingual multi-label tweet/X topic classification benchmark covering English, Spanish, Japanese, and Greek. The dataset contains 4,000 manually annotated tweets (1,000 per language) labeled with one or more of 19 social-media-oriented topics, extending the earlier English TweetTopic taxonomy. The paper details collection, preprocessing, annotation, agreement statistics, and descriptive analyses, then benchmarks zero-shot/few-shot LLMs and fine-tuned multilingual encoders under monolingual, cross-lingual, and multilingual settings. Results show the task is challenging, multilingual fine-tuning generally outperforms monolingual training, domain-specific tweet-pretrained encoders outperform generic multilingual encoders, and GPT-4o is competitive but generally not better than the best fine-tuned supervised models.

This paper introduces X-Topic, a multilingual multi-label tweet/X topic classification benchmark covering English, Spanish, Japanese, and Greek. The dataset contains 4,000 annotated tweets (1,000 per language) labeled with one or more of 19 social-media-oriented topics, using five annotators per tweet and a 2-of-5 agreement rule. The paper also provides descriptive analyses of topic distributions and overlaps, and benchmarks a range of approaches: zero-shot/few-shot LLMs, monolingual fine-tuning, cross-lingual transfer from the earlier English TweetTopic dataset, and multilingual fine-tuning. Results show that domain-specific multilingual encoders trained/fine-tuned on X data outperform generic multilingual models, multilingual training helps substantially over monolingual training, and GPT-4o is competitive in few-shot settings but generally does not surpass the best fine-tuned encoder models trained on all available data.

This paper proposes SyncLLM, a method for converting a pretrained autoregressive LLM (Llama3-8B) into a full-duplex spoken dialogue agent that can speak and listen synchronously rather than in turn-based fashion. The core idea is to inject coarse timing via periodic synchronization/speaker tokens and train the model on interleaved two-speaker speech-token streams, using deduplicated HuBERT tokens to preserve semantic density while retaining timing through chunk markers. To address real-time latency, the model predicts short future chunks for both speakers and uses an estimated current user chunk to generate its next response chunk, enabling robustness to one-chunk delays (160–240 ms). Training uses a three-stage recipe: synthetic turn-based spoken dialogue from text data, synthetic full-duplex dialogue without overlaps, and finally fine-tuning on ~2k hours of real spoken dialogue (Fisher), leveraging 212k hours of synthetic speech overall. Experiments show substantially better semantic quality than dGSLM, with human-rated meaningfulness improving by about 2.2 MOS points while maintaining similar naturalness of turn-taking; the model also shows reasonable out-of-distribution generalization and simulated interaction robustness under latency.

This paper proposes SyncLLM, a method for converting an autoregressive LLM (Llama3-8B) into a full-duplex spoken dialogue agent that can speak and listen synchronously rather than in strict turns. The core idea is to inject coarse timing via periodic synchronization/speaker tokens and train the model on interleaved, deduplicated HuBERT speech-unit sequences for both speakers. To address latency, the model predicts an estimated user chunk before generating its own next chunk, enabling operation under 160–240 ms delays. Training uses a three-stage recipe: large-scale synthetic spoken dialogue from text data, synthetic full-duplex data without overlaps, and finally ~2k hours of real spoken dialogue (Fisher). Experiments compare against dGSLM and show substantially better semantic coherence (lower ASR-transcribed perplexity, higher human meaningfulness MOS) while maintaining similar turn-taking naturalness, with some evidence of robustness to out-of-distribution data and simulated interaction between two SyncLLM agents.

This paper proposes an automated method to characterize NLI datasets into easy, ambiguous, and hard subsets using training dynamics. The approach extends dataset cartography by combining 8 features derived from two training settings—premise+hypothesis and hypothesis-only—and clustering examples with a Gaussian Mixture Model. Applied to SNLI, MultiNLI, and FEVER, the method identifies hard subsets with substantially lower model accuracy and reduced heuristic indicators of spurious correlations. The authors also show that applying the same characterization to training data can filter out uninformative examples and retain competitive performance using substantially less data, often outperforming prior training-dynamics-based selection methods.

The paper proposes an automated method to characterize NLI datasets into difficulty levels using training dynamics. It extends dataset cartography by combining 8 features derived from two training settings—premise+hypothesis and hypothesis-only—and clustering examples with a 3-component Gaussian Mixture Model into easy, ambiguous, and hard subsets. Experiments on SNLI, MultiNLI, and FEVER show that the hard subsets yield much lower model accuracy and reduced heuristic indicators of spurious correlations, while the same characterization applied to training data can retain comparable performance using substantially less data. The paper argues that this yields a more realistic and model-agnostic stress test for NLI than manually constructed adversarial sets.

This paper proposes CoT-Influx, a plug-and-play prompting method for improving LLM mathematical reasoning by fitting more useful few-shot chain-of-thought examples into a fixed context window. The method uses a coarse-to-fine pruner: a shot-level pruner first selects helpful CoT exemplars from a larger retrieved pool, and a token-level pruner then removes less important tokens while preserving reasoning-critical structure and numbers. Because pruning decisions are discrete and external to the frozen target LLM, the pruner is trained with REINFORCE using a reward that combines LLM loss, answer correctness, and token-budget constraints. The authors also construct MRD3, a GPT-4-generated/evolved math reasoning dataset with diverse difficulty levels and reasoning steps, used to train the pruner. Experiments on LLaMA2-7B/13B/70B across GSM8K, AddSub, MultiArith, SVAMP, and SingleEq show consistent gains over zero-shot, standard few-shot CoT, retrieval baselines, and prompt compression baselines. On GSM8K, CoT-Influx improves LLaMA2-70B to 59.59 EM, surpassing GPT-3.5 in the reported comparison.

This paper proposes CoT-Influx, a plug-and-play method to improve LLM mathematical reasoning by fitting more useful few-shot chain-of-thought examples into a fixed context window. The method uses a coarse-to-fine pruner: a shot-level pruner first selects helpful CoT exemplars from a larger retrieved pool, and a token-level pruner then removes less important tokens while preserving reasoning-critical structure and numbers. Because pruning decisions are discrete and external to the frozen target LLM, the authors train the pruner with REINFORCE using a reward that combines LLM loss, answer correctness, and token-budget compliance. They also construct MRD3, a GPT-4-generated/evolved math reasoning dataset with varied difficulty and reasoning depth, used for training and retrieval. Experiments on LLaMA2-7B/13B/70B across GSM8K, AddSub, MultiArith, SVAMP, and SingleEq show consistent gains over standard few-shot CoT, retrieval baselines, and prompt compression baselines, with the strongest headline result being LLaMA2-70B + CoT-Influx reaching 59.59 EM on GSM8K. The paper also includes ablations on the dataset, reward, and pruning stages, plus compatibility with self-consistency and self-verification.

This paper studies continual pre-training (CPT) of language models with mixed general and domain-specific data, aiming to identify an optimal domain-data proportion. The authors formalize a trade-off between preserving general capability and improving domain capability, define the feasible mixture-ratio set under a tolerance on general-loss degradation, and call the maximum feasible ratio the Critical Mixture Ratio (CMR). Empirically, using LLaMA-style models from 460M to 3.1B parameters and two domains (Finance and Academic Papers), they fit power-law style relationships between validation loss and (i) mixture ratio and (ii) training-token volume, then use these fits to predict CMR. They report that predicted CMR increases with model size and is larger when the target domain is closer to the original pre-training distribution.

This paper studies continual pre-training (CPT) of language models with mixed general and domain-specific data, aiming to identify an optimal domain-data mixture ratio. The authors define a Critical Mixture Ratio (CMR) as the largest mixture ratio that still preserves general-domain performance within a tolerance while improving domain loss. Empirically, using models from 460M to 3.1B parameters and two domains (Finance and Academic Papers), they fit power-law style relationships between loss and (i) mixture ratio and (ii) training token volume, then use these fits to predict CMR as a function of training budget. The main claim is that CMR exists, increases with model size and training budget, and depends on domain similarity to the original pre-training distribution.

This paper studies semantic information flow inside GPT-style transformers using logit-lens-style projections of hidden states and weights into vocabulary space. The authors focus especially on attention internals, arguing that attention values and a small number of dominant heads carry interpretable semantic content when projected appropriately through the OV circuit. Based on these observations, they introduce VISIT, an interactive flow-graph visualization tool that represents hidden states/neurons as nodes labeled by projected tokens and interactions as edges. The paper presents quantitative analyses on GPT-2-medium (with some validation on GPT-2-XL) using CounterFact prompts, plus qualitative case studies: reproducing aspects of indirect object identification circuits, suggesting layer norms act as semantic filters, and identifying frequently active 'regularization neurons' related to rogue dimensions.

This paper studies semantic information flow inside GPT-style transformers using vocabulary-space projections (logit lens). The authors analyze attention internals—especially values, heads, and their interaction with the OV circuit—and argue that only a small number of high-norm heads and high-attention memory values dominate the semantic contribution of an attention block. Building on these observations, they introduce VISIT, an interactive flow-graph visualization tool that represents hidden states and selected neurons as nodes labeled by projected tokens, with edges reflecting attention, activations, and residual accumulation. The paper presents qualitative case studies on GPT-2, including indirect object identification, a proposed semantic filtering role for layer norms, and the identification of frequently activated 'regularization neurons' related to rogue dimensions.

This paper presents a critical survey of sentiment analysis (SA) from a sociotechnical perspective. Reviewing 189 papers spanning applications, models, datasets, surveys, and frameworks, the authors argue that SA lacks clear, consistent, and interdisciplinary definitions of 'sentiment.' They show that SA has expanded from product reviews and finance into high-stakes domains such as healthcare and policymaking, while often relying on vague or inconsistent conceptualizations and heterogeneous measurement schemes. The paper also highlights transparency and accessibility issues in public SA models/datasets and discusses documented demographic biases. Based on these findings, it proposes four recommendations and a 10-question ethics sheet intended to guide more responsible development and deployment of SA systems.

This paper presents a critical survey of sentiment analysis (SA) from a sociotechnical perspective. Reviewing 189 papers spanning applications, models, datasets, surveys, and frameworks, the authors argue that SA lacks clear, consistent, and interdisciplinary definitions of 'sentiment.' They contrast technical uses of sentiment in NLP with social-scientific notions from psychology and sociology, showing that SA often conflates sentiment with opinion, emotion, and subjectivity. The survey further analyzes 60 application papers, 43 models, and 19 datasets, finding limited explicit definitions, heterogeneous measurement schemes, restricted transparency/accessibility, and documented demographic biases. Based on these observations, the paper proposes recommendations and a 10-question ethics sheet intended to guide more transparent, context-aware, and equitable development and deployment of SA systems.

This paper proposes Pushdown Layers, a drop-in replacement for Transformer self-attention that augments language models with an explicit stack-like memory represented as a "stack tape" of token depths in an incremental constituency parse. The model jointly predicts next tokens and attachment decisions, using supervised silver/gold parse annotations to update the stack tape and softly bias attention via depth embeddings added to keys. Experiments on Dyck languages, BLLIP sentence-level language modeling, and a newly constructed parsed Wikipedia corpus (WIKITREES) show improved syntactic generalization and better sample efficiency relative to standard Transformers, while maintaining similar perplexity. The paper also reports modest gains when finetuning GPT-2 with Pushdown Layers on several GLUE classification tasks.

This paper proposes Pushdown Layers, a drop-in replacement for Transformer self-attention that injects an explicit stack-like inductive bias for recursive structure. The method maintains a differentiable 'stack tape' encoding token depths in an incremental constituency parse, updates this tape autoregressively via an attachment head, and uses depth embeddings to modulate attention logits. The model is trained with silver or gold constituency supervision while preserving standard token-level LM outputs. Experiments on Dyck languages, BLLIP sentence-level language modeling, a newly constructed parsed Wikipedia corpus (WIKITREES), and GPT-2 finetuning show improved syntactic generalization and sample efficiency, with roughly comparable perplexity and modest downstream gains on some GLUE tasks.

This paper studies concept bottleneck models (CBMs) built on top of foundation model representations under test-time distribution shift. The authors argue that although CBMs can be interpretable and competitive on source-domain accuracy, they often degrade substantially after deployment under low-level, concept-level, and natural shifts. They formalize several failure modes—non-robust concept mappings, non-robust concept-to-label classifiers, and incomplete concept sets—and propose CONDA, a source-free test-time adaptation framework that updates the concept bank, the linear concept-to-label predictor, and an added residual concept bottleneck using only unlabeled target data and pseudo-labels derived from foundation-model-based zero-shot/linear-probe predictions. Experiments across CIFAR10/100-C, Waterbirds, Metashift, and Camelyon17 with multiple CBM construction methods show substantial target-domain gains in many settings, sometimes bringing CBM performance close to or above non-interpretable baselines while also yielding adapted concept explanations.

The paper studies test-time adaptation for concept bottleneck models (CBMs) built on top of foundation-model features under distribution shift. It argues that CBMs are not inherently robust after deployment, identifies three failure modes under low-level and concept-level shifts (non-robust concept mapping, non-robust classifier, incomplete concept set), and proposes CONDA, a three-stage source-free adaptation framework using only unlabeled target data: concept-score alignment (CSA), linear probing adaptation (LPA), and a residual concept bottleneck (RCB). Experiments on CIFAR10/100-C, Waterbirds, Metashift, and Camelyon17 with several CBM construction methods show substantial target-domain gains in many settings, sometimes bringing CBM performance close to or above non-interpretable zero-shot/linear-probe baselines, while also yielding qualitatively adapted concept explanations.

This paper presents Agent S, an open framework for autonomous GUI-based computer control using multimodal LLMs. The core idea is to combine (1) experience-augmented hierarchical planning, where a manager decomposes tasks into subtasks using retrieved web knowledge and narrative memory, (2) worker-level execution aided by episodic memory and trajectory reflection, and (3) an Agent-Computer Interface (ACI) that uses screenshots plus an augmented accessibility tree and a bounded primitive action space for grounding and control. The system also includes self-supervised exploration and continual memory updates via self-evaluation. On OSWorld, Agent S improves overall success rate from 11.21% (GPT-4o baseline) to 20.58%, with strong gains in Daily and Professional tasks; it also improves over a comparable setup on WindowsAgentArena from 13.3% to 18.2%.

This paper presents Agent S, an open framework for autonomous GUI-based computer control using multimodal LLMs. The core proposal combines three ideas: (1) experience-augmented hierarchical planning, where a manager decomposes tasks into subtasks using retrieved web knowledge and narrative memory, while workers execute subtasks using episodic memory; (2) continual memory construction and update via self-supervised exploration and self-evaluation; and (3) an Agent-Computer Interface (ACI) that uses screenshots plus an OCR-augmented accessibility tree and a bounded language-based action space for grounding and control. On OSWorld, Agent S improves over the reported GPT-4o baseline from 11.21% to 20.58% success rate, with gains across task categories; it also improves over a comparable setup on WindowsAgentArena from 13.3% to 18.2%. The paper includes ablations for retrieval, ACI, hierarchical planning, and memory update, plus qualitative examples and error analysis.

This paper introduces PSA (Private Steering for LLM Alignment), a simple differentially private activation-editing method for steering LLM behavior using private paired demonstrations. The method computes mean difference steering vectors between positive and negative demonstrations, clips per-example difference vectors, adds Gaussian noise to obtain private steering vectors, and then uses these vectors at inference time to steer selected layers. The authors provide a DP guarantee for the released steering vectors and argue that, by post-processing, infinitely many downstream generations incur no additional privacy cost. Empirically, they evaluate PSA on seven alignment-related behaviors across several open-source instruction-tuned LLMs (Llama-2, Mistral, Gemma, Qwen families), comparing against zero-shot, mean steering, and PCA steering. Results show PSA generally preserves much of the utility of non-private steering on behavioral MCQ tasks, GPT-4 judged open-ended generations, and MMLU. The paper also proposes a canary-based membership inference attack tailored to activation steering and shows that PSA reduces empirical leakage relative to non-private steering.

This paper studies privacy-preserving activation steering for LLM alignment. It proposes PSA, a simple method that computes mean steering vectors from paired positive/negative demonstrations, clips per-example activation differences, and adds Gaussian noise to obtain differentially private steering vectors. These private vectors are then injected at selected layers during inference, yielding formal DP guarantees for arbitrarily many downstream queries by post-processing. The paper evaluates PSA on seven alignment-related behaviors across several open-source instruction-tuned LLMs and compares against zero-shot, mean steering, and PCA-based steering. Results suggest PSA usually preserves much of the alignment utility and has limited impact on MMLU. The paper also introduces a canary-based membership inference attack tailored to activation steering and shows PSA reduces empirical leakage relative to non-private steering.

This paper formalizes auditing black-box LLM APIs as a two-sample hypothesis testing problem called Model Equality Testing: given samples from a reference distribution and an API, test whether they induce the same prompt-conditioned completion distribution. The authors propose kernel two-sample tests based on Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD), and empirically find that a simple Hamming/string kernel over completions is the most sample-efficient among several alternatives. In simulations across quantization, watermarking, finetuning, and model-swap perturbations, the method achieves strong power with relatively few samples, especially for long-form generation. The paper then audits 31 commercial endpoints serving Llama models and reports that 11 differ significantly from Meta reference weights (or fp16 variants), with some deviations large enough to rival swapping in a different model family. The work also uses estimated MMD as an effect-size notion to compare models and providers without log-probability access.

This paper formalizes auditing black-box LLM APIs as a two-sample hypothesis testing problem called Model Equality Testing: given samples from a reference model distribution and an API, test whether their prompt-conditioned completion distributions are equal. The authors propose kernel two-sample tests based on MMD, and empirically find that a simple Hamming/string kernel over completions is the most sample-efficient among several alternatives. In simulations across quantization, watermarking, finetuning, and model-swap settings, the Hamming-MMD test achieves strong power with relatively few samples (reported median 77.4% power at roughly 10 samples per prompt in their main setup). They then audit 31 commercial endpoints serving Llama models and report that 11 endpoints differ from Meta reference weights under their testing protocol. The paper also uses estimated MMD as an effect-size measure to compare models and APIs.

The paper studies reward overoptimization in offline RLHF and argues that it arises from distribution shift plus uncertainty in learned preference rewards. It proposes a theoretical maximin objective that selects a policy against an adversarial reward model minimizing MLE loss plus a reward penalty. Under regularity assumptions, this objective is shown equivalent to a practical minimax reformulation that yields a simple training loss: DPO-style preference optimization plus an imitation/SFT loss, called Regularized Preference Optimization (RPO). The paper proves an O(1/sqrt(N)) style suboptimality guarantee under a partial coverage assumption and presents experiments on Zephyr beta/gemma style 7B models showing improved chosen-response log-probability during training, better GPT-4 judged pairwise win rates on held-out in-distribution prompts, and modest gains on MT-Bench, AlpacaEval 2.0, and some math/reasoning/coding benchmarks.

The paper studies reward overoptimization in RLHF through an offline contextual bandit formulation with Bradley-Terry preferences. It proposes a theoretical maximin algorithm that selects a policy against an adversarially chosen reward model minimizing a combination of preference-model MLE loss and a reward penalty term, under a partial-coverage assumption. The authors then derive an equivalent minimax formulation and, via the reward-policy equivalence used in DPO-style methods, obtain a practical objective called Regularized Preference Optimization (RPO): DPO loss plus an imitation/SFT loss on a baseline distribution. The theory gives an \~O(1/sqrt(N)) suboptimality guarantee under general function approximation and partial coverage, and a generalization result to shifted prompt distributions under bounded density ratio assumptions. Empirically, on Zephyr beta and gemma training setups, RPO appears to reduce the drop in log-probability on chosen responses during training and modestly improves GPT-4-judged in-distribution pairwise win rates, MT-Bench, AlpacaEval 2.0, and some math/reasoning/coding benchmarks over DPO baselines.

This paper studies motion forecasting under a more realistic continuous-driving setting, arguing that standard benchmarks and methods treat each scene independently and therefore ignore useful temporal relationships across successive scenes. The authors propose RealMotion, which combines: (1) a scene context stream that recurrently carries forward scene-level context across sub-scenes using alignment and cross-attention, and (2) an agent trajectory stream that stores past predicted trajectories/features in a memory bank and refines current predictions via trajectory-conditioned attention. To support this setting on existing benchmarks, they reorganize each original scene into a sequence of sub-scenes by splitting trajectories at multiple historical timestamps and aggregating local context around each split point. Experiments on Argoverse 1 and 2, including multi-agent forecasting, show improved leaderboard performance over prior methods, with ablations suggesting gains from both the data reorganization and the two temporal streams, while maintaining relatively low online inference latency.

This paper studies motion forecasting under a more realistic continuous-driving setting, arguing that standard benchmarks and methods treat each scene independently and therefore ignore useful temporal continuity across successive scenes. The authors propose RealMotion, which combines: (1) a scene context stream that aligns and propagates scene-level features over time via cross-attention, and (2) an agent trajectory stream that stores past predicted trajectories/features in a memory bank and refines current predictions through trajectory-conditioned attention. They also introduce a data reorganization strategy that converts standard benchmark scenes into short continuous sub-scene sequences by splitting trajectories at multiple historical timestamps. Experiments on Argoverse 1 and 2, including multi-agent forecasting, show improvements over prior methods and over an internal independent baseline, with additional ablations on the contributions of the data reorganization, alignment, trajectory embedding, split points, and block depth. The method also reports favorable parameter count and online latency relative to some baselines.

The paper studies how QAOA performance depends on mixer Hamiltonian design and circuit depth, arguing that the best parameter-grouping strategy is both problem- and depth-dependent. It presents a theoretical analysis based on symmetry/effective-dimension arguments and proposes MG-Net, a two-stage deep learning framework that first learns a cost estimator for QAOA performance and then trains a generator to output mixer Hamiltonians conditioned on the problem instance and allowed depth. Experiments on weighted Max-Cut and transverse-field Ising model instances, including simulations up to 64 qubits, show improved approximation ratios and optimization behavior over standard QAOA, multi-angle QAOA, ADAPT-QAOA, and some classical baselines.

The paper studies how QAOA performance depends on mixer Hamiltonian design and circuit depth, arguing that the best parameter-grouping strategy is both problem- and depth-dependent. It presents a theoretical analysis relating convergence to symmetry/effective dimension and proposes MG-Net, a two-stage graph-based learning framework that predicts customized mixer Hamiltonians from a problem instance and target depth. Experiments on weighted Max-Cut and TFIM, including simulations up to 64 qubits, show improved approximation ratios and faster optimization relative to standard QAOA, multi-angle QAOA, ADAPT-QAOA, and some classical baselines.

This paper studies hybrid reinforcement learning in episodic linear MDPs, where an agent can use both an offline dataset and online interaction, without assuming single-policy concentrability of the behavior policy. It proposes two computationally efficient algorithms: RAPPEL, an online-to-offline method that performs reward-agnostic exploration and then pessimistic offline RL for PAC policy learning; and HYRULE, an offline-to-online method that warm-starts an optimistic online RL algorithm for regret minimization. The main theoretical claims are that RAPPEL achieves PAC/error bounds that are never worse than the best known offline-only guarantees and can improve on them, while HYRULE achieves regret bounds never worse than minimax-optimal online-only guarantees and can improve on them when offline data is useful. The analysis is based on partitioning the feature/state-action space into offline-covered and online-explored components, yielding bounds in terms of partial concentrability/coverability quantities and reduced effective dimensions. The paper also includes small-scale experiments on a Tetris-like environment showing empirical benefits of hybridization in both settings.

The paper studies hybrid reinforcement learning in episodic linear MDPs, where an agent has both an offline dataset and a budget of online interaction. It proposes two computationally efficient algorithms tailored to two hybrid-RL paradigms: (1) RAPPEL, an online-to-offline method that performs reward-agnostic exploration to augment offline data and then runs pessimistic offline RL for PAC policy learning; and (2) HYRULE, an offline-to-online method that warm-starts an optimistic online RL algorithm with estimates from offline data for regret minimization. The main theoretical claim is that, without assuming single-policy concentrability, these methods achieve bounds that are never worse than the best known offline-only or online-only guarantees in linear MDPs and can strictly improve on them depending on the quality/quantity of offline and online data. The paper also provides limited experiments on a scaled-down Tetris environment illustrating improved coverage, better policy value for the online-to-offline approach, and lower regret for the warm-started online method.

The paper proposes Efficient Safe Policy Optimization (ESPO), an on-policy primal safe RL method that improves sample efficiency by dynamically adjusting sample size based on reward-cost gradient conflict. ESPO builds on a three-mode optimization framework: reward-only updates when safely feasible, cost-only updates under clear violations, and joint reward-cost updates in a soft-constraint region, with projected gradients used when reward and safety gradients conflict. The paper provides convergence analysis in a tabular softmax-policy setting, argues reduced oscillation relative to CRPO/PCRPO, and claims improved sample efficiency from adaptive sample manipulation. Empirically, ESPO is evaluated on Safety-MuJoCo and Omnisafe tasks and is reported to achieve better reward/safety trade-offs while using fewer samples and less training time than several primal and primal-dual baselines.

The paper proposes Efficient Safe Policy Optimization (ESPO), an on-policy safe reinforcement learning method for CMDPs that aims to improve sample efficiency by dynamically adjusting sample size based on reward-cost gradient conflict. ESPO builds on a three-mode optimization framework: reward-only updates when constraints are comfortably satisfied, cost-only updates when constraints are violated, and joint reward-cost updates in a soft-constraint region, with projected gradients used under conflict. The main claimed contribution is a conflict-aware sample manipulation rule that increases sample size when reward and safety gradients conflict and decreases it otherwise. The paper provides convergence analysis in a tabular softmax-policy setting, argues reduced oscillation relative to CRPO/PCRPO, and presents experiments on Safety-MuJoCo and Omnisafe showing improved reward, safety, and reduced sample usage/training time versus several primal and primal-dual baselines.

The paper proposes GraphMETRO, a graph neural network framework for out-of-distribution generalization under complex and heterogeneous graph distribution shifts. The core idea is to model an unknown target shift as a mixture of predefined stochastic shift components, using a gating network to infer instance-specific shift mixtures and multiple expert networks to produce representations invariant to individual components. A reference expert and an alignment loss are introduced so expert outputs lie in a common representation space. Experiments on four GOOD benchmark datasets (WebKB, Twitch, Twitter, SST2) and several synthetic datasets show improved performance over ERM and prior graph OOD baselines, with especially large gains on WebKB. The paper also includes ablations on alignment and expert sharing, plus qualitative analyses such as invariance matrices and inferred shift mixtures.

The paper proposes GraphMETRO, a graph out-of-distribution generalization method for complex and heterogeneous distribution shifts. The core idea is to decompose unknown graph shifts into a mixture of predefined stochastic shift components, use a gating GNN to infer instance-specific component weights, and combine multiple expert GNNs that each learn representations invariant to one shift component. A reference expert and an alignment loss are introduced so expert outputs lie in a shared representation space. Experiments on four GOOD benchmark datasets (WebKB, Twitch, Twitter, SST2) and several synthetic datasets show improved performance over ERM and prior graph OOD baselines, with especially large gains on WebKB. The paper also includes ablations on alignment, shared-vs-separate experts, and transform choices, plus qualitative analyses of inferred shift mixtures and expert invariance.

The paper develops general asymptotic lower and upper bounds on the KL divergence between a full Bayesian posterior and its coreset approximation, aiming to cover settings beyond exponential families or strongly log-concave smooth models. The lower bounds (Theorems 3.3 and 3.5) rely on mild local regularity and posterior concentration assumptions and are used to show fundamental limitations of importance-weighted coresets, including that such methods generally require coreset size proportional to dataset size to maintain bounded error, and that any coreset method needs more than d points in locally d-dimensional settings. The upper bound (Theorem 5.3) is based on a generalized subexponentiality condition on centered log-likelihoods and is applied to subsample-optimize methods, yielding bounded-error guarantees with polylogarithmic coreset size under additional alignment assumptions. Experiments on two challenging synthetic models with multimodality, unidentifiability, and heavy tails support the theoretical predictions.

The paper develops general lower and upper bounds on the KL divergence between a full Bayesian posterior and its coreset approximation, aiming to cover settings beyond exponential families and strongly log-concave smooth models. The main theoretical contributions are broad asymptotic lower bounds (Theorems 3.3 and 3.5) under mild local regularity and concentration assumptions, and an upper bound (Theorem 5.3) based on a generalized multivariate subexponentiality condition. These results are then used to derive concrete implications for coreset construction methods: importance-weighted subsampling coresets require size proportional to dataset size to maintain bounded error, any coreset method needs at least more than d points in a locally d-parameter setting, and subsample-optimize methods can achieve bounded error with polylogarithmic coreset size under suitable assumptions. Experiments on two challenging synthetic models—a multimodal/unidentifiable Cauchy location model and an unidentifiable heavy-tailed logistic regression model—support the qualitative theoretical predictions.
